before.content_html:
Why Finance Matters

Every business needs money to operate. A start-up needs cash to rent premises, buy stock and pay its first wage packet. An established business needs money to replace worn-out vehicles, launch new products or open new branches. Finance is the fuel that keeps a business alive — and picking the wrong source can be the difference between growth and going bust.

The question is not just ‘where does the money come from?’ but ‘which source is the best fit?’ A new sole trader with no trading history will struggle to get a bank loan but might raise cash from family. A plc like Tesco can issue new shares on the stock market — something a sole trader cannot legally do.

Internal Sources of Finance

Internal finance comes from inside the business. There are three main sources.

Retained profit — profit the business has made and kept back rather than paid out to owners. It is free: no interest, no repayment, no loss of control. The downside is that a new business has no profit yet, and using retained profit means the owners receive less income this year.

Selling unwanted assets — a business sells off spare machinery, an old van, or a property it no longer uses. This frees up cash quickly, but only works if the business actually owns something worth selling, and the asset cannot be recovered if the business needs it later.

Owner’s savings — the entrepreneur puts personal money into the business. Cheap and quick, but risky for the owner: if the business fails they lose their savings as well as their income.

Key Fact

Internal sources — retained profit, selling unwanted assets, owner’s savings — do not involve borrowing or outside investors. They cost nothing in interest, but the business has to already have the money or the asset to use them.

External Sources of Finance

External finance comes from outside the business. The AQA specification requires seven main sources.

Family and friends — informal loans or gifts from people who know the owner. Often interest-free and flexible, but arguments over repayment can wreck relationships.

New share issue — a Ltd or plc sells new shares to investors in exchange for cash. Large amounts can be raised with no repayment date, but ownership is diluted — existing owners control a smaller slice of the business. Only limited companies can do this; a sole trader cannot.

Bank loan — the bank lends a fixed sum to be repaid with interest over an agreed period. Good for large one-off purchases like a delivery van. The business must pay interest and may need to offer collateral.

Mortgage — a long-term loan secured against property. Used to buy premises. Interest is usually lower than a normal loan because the property acts as security, but the property can be repossessed if repayments are missed.

Overdraft — the bank lets the business spend more than is in its current account, up to an agreed limit. Flexible for short-term cash-flow problems, but interest rates are high and the bank can demand repayment at any time.

Trade credit — a supplier delivers stock now and lets the business pay 30, 60 or 90 days later. Effectively an interest-free short-term loan, but late payment damages the supplier relationship.

Hire purchase — the business pays for an asset in monthly instalments and owns it at the end. Spreads the cost, but the total paid is more than the cash price.

Government grants — cash from a government scheme, often for start-ups in deprived areas or green-technology firms. Free money, but grants are competitive, come with strict conditions and take time to apply for.

Choosing the Right Source

Innocent Smoothies is a classic UK example. Three Cambridge graduates started it in 1999 with £500 of fruit. They grew via small business loans and, years later, crowdfunded rounds and a share sale to Coca-Cola. Early on they had no trading history — a bank would not lend them six-figure sums, so they relied on a mix of owner’s savings and family support. As the business grew, it could access loans, new share issues and eventually sell a stake to a global giant.

The suitability of a source depends on four things: how much is needed, how quickly, for how long, and how established the business is. A £2,000 emergency tax bill might be covered by an overdraft. A £200,000 factory expansion needs a mortgage or new share issue, not an overdraft.

Key Fact

New share issues are only available to limited companies (Ltd and plc). Sole traders and partnerships cannot sell shares — they rely on savings, retained profit, loans, overdrafts and trade credit instead.

Short-term vs Long-term Finance

Another way of thinking about sources is how long the business needs the money. Short-term finance (under a year) covers temporary cash needs: an overdraft to bridge a quiet month, trade credit for a bulk stock order, or an owner’s savings injection to cover wages. Long-term finance (over a year) funds big projects that will pay back over time: a mortgage on new premises, a bank loan for a delivery van fleet, or a share issue for an overseas expansion. Matching the length of the finance to the length of the need matters — paying for a 10-year factory extension with a 12-month overdraft is a recipe for disaster when the bank demands repayment.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal finance (retained profit, selling assets, owner’s savings) costs no interest but needs the business to already have the money or asset.
  • External finance includes family/friends, new share issues, loans, mortgages, overdrafts, trade credit, hire purchase and government grants — each with different costs, risks and conditions.
  • The right source depends on the amount, the time frame, the length of the need and the business’s legal structure. Innocent Smoothies started with savings, grew via loans, then used share issues.

before.exam_tip_html: AQA will not ask you to construct a whole cash-flow forecast — but they will ask you to interpret one or fill in missing cells. For 3-mark ‘Calculate’ questions, always show the working (inflow − outflow, or opening balance + net cash flow) even if you can do it in your head. The method mark is half the total. For 6-mark ‘Analyse’ and 12-mark ‘Evaluate’ questions on cash flow, the marker is looking for chains of reasoning — explain why a negative closing balance threatens survival, not just that it does.
before.content_html:
Cash Keeps a Business Alive

A business can be profitable on paper and still collapse if it runs out of cash. Wages, rent and supplier bills all have to be paid in actual money on the day they fall due — the tax office and the landlord do not accept IOUs. Cash flow is the movement of money into and out of a business over time. If more is going out than coming in for too long, the business becomes insolvent and folds.

This is why the biggest conceptual trap in Finance is assuming profit and cash are the same thing. A sale generates profit the moment it is made, but the cash may not arrive for 30, 60 or 90 days if the customer is on trade credit. Meanwhile the business still has to pay wages every Friday.

Key Fact

Profit is not the same as cash. A business can be profitable and still fail if cash is not available to pay wages, rent and suppliers on the day they are due. Cash is about timing; profit is about the full trading year.

Reading a Cash-Flow Forecast

A cash-flow forecast is a table that predicts cash in and cash out, month by month. Students are not expected to build one from scratch, but interpreting one is core AQA content. The four key rows are:

Cash inflows — money coming in from sales, loans, investment or asset sales.

Cash outflows — money going out on wages, rent, stock, utilities, loan repayments.

Net cash flow — inflows minus outflows for that month. It can be positive or negative. \(\text{Net cash flow} = \text{Total inflows} - \text{Total outflows}\)

Opening and closing balances — the opening balance is how much cash the business had at the start of the month. The closing balance is opening balance + net cash flow, and it becomes the next month’s opening balance.

Worked Example — A Cornish Surf Shop

A surf shop in Newquay starts January with a cash balance of £8,000 (the opening balance). In January it receives £12,000 from sales (inflow) and pays out £15,000 in wages, rent and stock (outflow).

Step 1 — net cash flow:

$$\text{Net cash flow} = \pounds12{,}000 - \pounds15{,}000 = -\pounds3{,}000$$

Step 2 — closing balance:

$$\text{Closing balance} = \pounds8{,}000 + (-\pounds3{,}000) = \pounds5{,}000$$

The shop ends January with £5,000 in the bank. Still positive — but if February repeats the same £3,000 shortfall, the balance falls to £2,000, and by March the shop is overdrawn. Retail often shows this seasonal pattern: Dunelm, the UK homeware chain, sees its heaviest sales in spring/summer and has to manage tighter cash in quieter months.

Key Fact

Closing balance = Opening balance + Net cash flow. Net cash flow = Cash inflows − Cash outflows. The closing balance of one month is the opening balance of the next.

Why Too Much Cash Is Also a Problem

Most students see cash-flow problems as ‘not enough cash’. That is only half the story. Holding too much idle cash is also wasteful because of opportunity cost. Cash sitting in a current account earns almost no interest. The same money, invested in new stock, marketing, or a savings product, could have been earning a return. Experienced managers aim for enough cash to pay bills comfortably — not a pile sitting idle.

Fixing a Cash-Flow Problem

When a forecast shows a shortfall, the business has four main levers.

Re-scheduling payments — negotiate longer trade credit with suppliers or delay non-urgent bills. Low risk, but can damage supplier relationships if overused.

Arrange an overdraft — short-term bank facility for a dip. Quick and flexible, but interest is high and the bank can withdraw the facility.

Reduce cash outflow — cut non-essential spending, renegotiate rent, switch to cheaper suppliers, reduce stock held. Takes longer to bite but has no borrowing cost.

Increase cash inflow — chase unpaid invoices, offer discounts for early payment, run a promotion. The right fix, but depends on customer response and may squeeze profit margins.

Matching the Fix to the Problem

A good manager picks the right solution for the right problem. A one-off dip — say a major customer pays late by a fortnight — is what overdrafts are designed for. A structural problem — outflows consistently higher than inflows — cannot be fixed by borrowing, because the debt just grows. That needs cost cutting, price changes or finding new sources of revenue. Dunelm, the UK homeware retailer, faces predictable seasonality: sales peak in spring/summer when people refresh their homes, then dip through autumn. Rather than constantly juggling overdrafts, Dunelm plans supplier payment terms and stock levels around the pattern, keeping cash healthy year-round. The lesson is the same at any scale: forecast first, then use the right tool for the specific shortfall. A small business might use a mix — rescheduling a couple of supplier invoices, asking customers to pay faster, and keeping a small overdraft as backup — rather than relying on any single solution.

before.exam_tip_html: Calculation questions are where Business students most often lose easy marks. AQA does not give you the formulae in the exam — you have to memorise them. Always show your working: method marks are awarded even if the final number is wrong. Always add the correct unit (£ or %) to the final answer — a bare number loses a mark. For ‘Explain’ questions on costs, a definition alone is not enough — you need a because clause showing why the cost behaves that way.

AQA will not give you the formulae for break-even or ARR — memorise them. For break-even questions, always calculate contribution per unit first, then divide fixed costs by that figure. For ARR, the two-step order matters: find average annual profit first, then divide by initial investment and multiply by 100. Add the % sign — forgetting it loses a mark. For ‘Evaluate’ questions on break-even, acknowledge its weaknesses: it assumes all units sell at the same price and ignores changes in variable cost per unit as output scales.
before.content_html:
What Break-Even Actually Means

Before a business can make a profit, it has to cover all its costs — both fixed and variable. Break-even is the exact level of sales where total revenue equals total costs. One unit fewer and the business is in loss; one unit more and it starts making profit.

For managers, break-even is not abstract theory — it’s a target. A coffee shop owner who knows she needs to sell 220 lattes a week to break even can plan opening hours, staffing and marketing around that number. If she reliably beats that figure, she’s profitable.

The Two Break-Even Formulae

AQA requires interpretation of break-even charts, not drawing them from scratch. But the underlying numbers come from two formulae. The first gives the break-even point in units:

$$\text{Break-even (units)} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs}}{\text{Contribution per unit}}$$

Contribution per unit is the selling price minus the variable cost per unit:

$$\text{Contribution} = \text{Selling price} - \text{Variable cost per unit}$$

To convert break-even units into a revenue figure:

$$\text{Break-even (revenue)} = \text{Break-even units} \times \text{Selling price}$$

Worked Example — Oakleaf Coffee Again

Fictional Oakleaf Coffee sells lattes at £3.50. Variable cost per latte is £1.10, and fixed costs are £1,200 a week. How many lattes does Oakleaf need to sell to break even?

Step 1 — contribution per latte:

$$\text{Contribution} = \pounds3.50 - \pounds1.10 = \pounds2.40$$

Step 2 — break-even (units):

$$\text{Break-even} = \frac{\pounds1{,}200}{\pounds2.40} = 500 \text{ lattes per week}$$

Oakleaf needs to sell 500 lattes per week to cover every penny of fixed and variable costs. Anything above 500 is profit. Anything below is loss.

Key Fact

Break-even (units) = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Contribution = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Every unit sold above the break-even point is pure profit.

Margin of Safety

The margin of safety shows how far a business can afford its sales to fall before it starts making a loss. It’s calculated as:

$$\text{Margin of safety} = \text{Actual sales} - \text{Break-even sales}$$

If Oakleaf actually sells 650 lattes a week (break-even is 500), the margin of safety is 150 lattes. Sales could drop by up to 150 before the shop starts losing money. A healthy margin of safety gives the business a cushion against bad weather, rivals opening nearby, or a general dip in demand.

If fixed costs rise — say rent increases by £300 a week — the break-even point rises because the numerator in the formula is bigger. Oakleaf would now need to sell £1,500 ÷ £2.40 = 625 lattes per week, not 500.

If selling price rises — say the latte goes up to £4.00 — contribution becomes £4.00 − £1.10 = £2.90. Break-even falls to £1,200 ÷ £2.90 = 414 lattes. The shop has to sell fewer units because each one contributes more.

If variable costs rise — say milk prices go up, pushing variable cost to £1.40 — contribution falls to £2.10. Break-even rises to £1,200 ÷ £2.10 = 572 lattes.

Investment Decisions: Average Rate of Return

Businesses don’t only use break-even. When weighing up a one-off investment project — a new delivery van, a factory extension, a coffee roaster — managers calculate the average rate of return (ARR). ARR turns a total profit figure into an annual percentage so it can be compared to savings rates or other investments.

The formula is:

$$\text{ARR} = \frac{\text{Total profit from project} \div \text{years}}{\text{Initial investment}} \times 100$$

Worked Example — Buying a New Coffee Roaster

Oakleaf spends £20,000 on a new roaster. Over five years it generates £30,000 of profit in total. The ARR is:

$$\text{Average annual profit} = \frac{\pounds30{,}000}{5} = \pounds6{,}000$$

$$\text{ARR} = \frac{\pounds6{,}000}{\pounds20{,}000} \times 100 = 30\%$$

A 30% ARR comfortably beats bank savings (around 4-5% currently). The investment looks strong. If Oakleaf had a rival project offering 45% ARR, she would pick that instead — assuming the risk was similar.

Key Fact

ARR = (Total profit ÷ years) ÷ Initial investment × 100. It gives the average annual return as a percentage. It does NOT take timing of returns or the risk of the project into account — these have to be considered separately.

Strengths: ARR is simple to calculate and easy to explain to non-finance staff. It produces a percentage, which can be compared directly with interest rates on savings, loans or alternative investments. It uses the full life of a project, not just the first year or two.

Weaknesses: ARR averages profits over the whole project, ignoring when the returns arrive — a project paying big profits in year 1 is treated the same as one paying them in year 5, even though money now is worth more than money later. ARR is also based on forecasts that may be wildly wrong, and it ignores the level of risk attached to a project. A 30% ARR on a reckless venture is worse than a 15% ARR on a safe one.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Break-even = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Every unit sold above this point is pure profit; every unit below is loss.
  • Margin of safety = Actual sales − Break-even sales. It measures how much sales can fall before the business starts losing money.
  • ARR = (Total profit ÷ years) ÷ Initial investment × 100. It turns a project’s total profit into an annual percentage for comparison with alternatives.

before.content_html:
Why Businesses Publish Financial Statements

Every limited company in the UK has to publish financial statements each year. Investors read them before buying shares. Banks read them before lending. Managers read them to decide next year’s strategy. Employees read them to judge whether their jobs are safe. The two core documents are the income statement and the statement of financial position.

The Income Statement

The income statement (sometimes called the profit and loss account) covers a period of time — usually a full trading year. It starts with revenue at the top and works down through costs to arrive at profit at the bottom.

Revenue — the total money taken from sales over the period.

Cost of sales — the direct cost of producing what was sold (materials, direct labour, stock used).

Gross profit — revenue minus cost of sales. It shows how much money is made on the products themselves, before running costs.

Other operating costs — rent, marketing, office salaries, utilities. The overheads of running the business.

Net profit (profit for the year) — gross profit minus all other costs (including any finance costs and tax). The bottom line.

The Statement of Financial Position

The statement of financial position (balance sheet) is different. It is a snapshot in time — what the business owns and owes on one specific date, usually the last day of the trading year. The income statement is a film of the year; the statement of financial position is a photo at year-end.

Its two key categories are assets and liabilities. Assets are things the business owns — premises, vehicles, stock, cash in the bank, invoices owed by customers. Liabilities are what the business owes — bank loans, mortgages, unpaid invoices from suppliers.

Key Fact

Income statement = performance over a period (usually a year). Statement of financial position = a snapshot of what the business owns and owes at one point in time. One is a film, the other is a photo.

Profit Margins: Measuring Efficiency

Raw profit figures are hard to compare between businesses. A corner shop making £20,000 profit on £100,000 of sales is doing a great job. Tesco making £20,000 profit would be a disaster. That’s why managers convert profit into profit margin — a percentage that strips out the size of the business.

There are two core margin calculations in the AQA spec. Gross profit margin:

$$\text{Gross profit margin} = \frac{\text{Gross profit}}{\text{Revenue}} \times 100$$

Net profit margin:

$$\text{Net profit margin} = \frac{\text{Net profit}}{\text{Revenue}} \times 100$$

Worked Example — A Fashion Retailer

A UK fashion retailer reports revenue of £500,000, cost of sales of £300,000, and other operating costs of £150,000.

Step 1 — gross profit:

$$\text{Gross profit} = \pounds500{,}000 - \pounds300{,}000 = \pounds200{,}000$$

Step 2 — net profit:

$$\text{Net profit} = \pounds200{,}000 - \pounds150{,}000 = \pounds50{,}000$$

Step 3 — margins:

$$\text{Gross profit margin} = \frac{\pounds200{,}000}{\pounds500{,}000} \times 100 = 40\%$$

$$\text{Net profit margin} = \frac{\pounds50{,}000}{\pounds500{,}000} \times 100 = 10\%$$

The 30-percentage-point gap between gross (40%) and net (10%) margin tells a story: the business is making decent money on its products, but overheads are eating most of it. A manager looking at these figures would probe rent, marketing spend and head-office salaries.

Key Fact

Gross profit margin = (Gross profit ÷ Revenue) × 100. Net profit margin = (Net profit ÷ Revenue) × 100. A large gap between them shows high overheads eating into the profit made on the products themselves.

Making Judgements

Just calculating a margin isn’t enough — the figure only has meaning in context. Managers compare performance against:

Previous years — is gross profit margin rising or falling? A falling margin suggests rising supplier costs or price cuts that haven’t been passed on. A rising one suggests better buying power or a premium brand position.

Competitors — how does the margin compare to rivals in the same sector? Supermarkets typically run net margins of 2-5%. Luxury brands like Burberry run 15-20%. Context decides whether a number is good or bad.

Different stakeholders read financial statements differently. Shareholders want rising margins. Employees want stable profits that secure jobs. Suppliers want healthy cash reserves that mean the business will pay its bills. No single figure answers every question.

Shareholders look at net profit margin and total profit — rising figures mean bigger dividends or a share price rise. Falling figures prompt awkward questions at the annual general meeting.

Managers look at the gap between gross and net profit margin to spot whether overheads are rising faster than product costs. They use the statement to decide where to cut costs or raise prices.

Employees and trade unions look at overall profitability — a loss-making year signals redundancy risk; a strongly profitable year is ammunition in pay negotiations.

Suppliers check the statement of financial position for assets and cash reserves — they want reassurance that invoices will be paid on time before extending trade credit to the business.
